### <a id="llm-attention"></a>1. Derive scaled dot-product attention and explain how its scale affects softmax gradients.

*Knowledge · [LLM fundamentals](../themes/llm-fundamentals.md) · [Checklist](../themes/llm-fundamentals.md#llm-attention)*

For self-attention, Q, K and V have dimensions batch, heads, sequence length and head width. I multiply Q by transposed K, divide scores by the square root of key width, apply softmax over keys and multiply by V. The output matches Q's shape when value and key widths match; cross-attention may use different query and key lengths. Scaling controls growing dot-product variance, which can saturate softmax and weaken gradients. For causal attention, future positions receive minus infinity before softmax; subtracting each row's maximum improves numerical stability. I'd compare against a reference on random tensors and verify that changing future tokens cannot change earlier outputs. Scaling alone cannot prevent every low-precision overflow, and it does not replace normalisation.

Read: [Attention Is All You Need](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="llm-kv-cache"></a>2. Derive the memory required by a decoder's KV cache as batch size and context length grow.

*Knowledge · [LLM fundamentals](../themes/llm-fundamentals.md) · [Checklist](../themes/llm-fundamentals.md#llm-kv-cache)*

With equal lengths the size is 2 × batch × layers × tokens × KV heads × head width × bytes per element. The two is keys and values; queries aren't kept, because the current step's Q is needed for exactly one iteration, while the keys and values of every past position are read again at each following step. The cache grows linearly in both batch and context length, so on long conversations it can limit concurrency beyond the weight budget. To that formula you always add weights, activations and working buffers, allocator headroom, and padding waste when lengths differ and memory is handed out as a rectangle; paged allocation, as in PagedAttention, reduces that fragmentation. I'd compute the budget over the real length distribution and reconcile it with measured memory under load. The formula ignores cache compression, offload and architectures that store the cache differently.

Read: [Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.06180) · [GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models from Multi-Head Checkpoints](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.13245)

### <a id="llm-grouped-query"></a>3. Compare multi-head, multi-query and grouped-query attention in quality and serving memory.

*Knowledge · [LLM fundamentals](../themes/llm-fundamentals.md) · [Checklist](../themes/llm-fundamentals.md#llm-grouped-query)*

The distinction is the number of KV heads per query head: in MHA every query head has its own K and V pair, in MQA all query heads share a single pair, in GQA the heads are split into groups and the pair is shared inside a group. KV head count enters the cache formula linearly, so MQA gives the smallest cache and the least memory read per step, and small batch decode is bound by exactly that reading. We pay in quality: MQA can lose more quality; GQA can stay closer to MHA. From an existing MHA checkpoint you average the KV heads within groups and fine-tune on a small fraction of the original budget, so the move isn't free. I'd measure both cache per sequence and quality on my own eval set, alongside speed. With short prompts and large batches the gain is smaller: the bottleneck is elsewhere.

Read: [GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models from Multi-Head Checkpoints](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.13245)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="llm-compute-optimal"></a>4. Under a fixed training compute budget, how do Chinchilla-style scaling results change the balance between model size and training tokens?

*Knowledge · [LLM fundamentals](../themes/llm-fundamentals.md) · [Checklist](../themes/llm-fundamentals.md#llm-compute-optimal)*

Chinchilla shows that under a fixed compute budget parameter count and training tokens have to grow together, whereas earlier practice took too large a model and too little data. The relationship is empirical, fitted over many runs of different sizes, so carrying its coefficients over to another architecture, tokeniser or corpus deserves caution. The main trade-off is that the training optimum is not the serving optimum: if the model will serve an enormous stream of requests, you're better off with fewer parameters trained longer on more tokens, paying in training time and winning on every request for years. I'd work out total cost of ownership, training plus projected inference over the model's lifetime, and separately check whether there's enough quality data without harmful duplication. The law says nothing about post-training, about limited corpora, or about whether the quality you need is reachable at all.

Read: [Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15556)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="llm-context-position"></a>5. How would you test and reduce a model's tendency to miss relevant evidence in the middle of a long context?

*Knowledge · [LLM fundamentals](../themes/llm-fundamentals.md) · [Checklist](../themes/llm-fundamentals.md#llm-context-position)*

You test it by moving the evidence: take a question whose answer sits in exactly one passage and slide that passage through input positions, changing nothing else. A dip in the middle with identical content is the positional effect, not a shortage of context. Measure at several input lengths, with varying numbers of similar distractor passages, and separately for each model: the behaviour depends on training and on length, and window size on its own promises nothing. Three things soften the problem: retrieve more precisely so there's less text to read; rerank and place strong candidates nearer the edges; shrink the context by summarising or dropping what isn't needed. I'd put a positional slice into the regular eval set and recheck it on every model change. There's no universal cure: long context stays more expensive in money and latency, and it doesn't replace good retrieval.

Read: [Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="inf-prefill-decode"></a>6. Contrast prefill with autoregressive decode and explain when compute or memory bandwidth becomes the bottleneck.

*Knowledge · [Inference, serving and cost](../themes/inference-economics.md) · [Checklist](../themes/inference-economics.md#inf-prefill-decode)*

Prefill computes all prompt positions in one pass and fills large matrix blocks, so it's usually compute bound. Decode runs autoregressively, one token per iteration: every step has to read all the weights of a layer to do arithmetic over a single token per sequence, so at small batch the arithmetic intensity is low and memory bandwidth becomes the limit. Batching moves that boundary: the more sequences run together, the better the weights you've read are reused and the closer decode gets to the compute limit, but the KV cache grows and so does reading the cache itself. So before any optimisation I'd take a profile on the real distribution of prompt and output lengths and look per phase at achieved memory bandwidth and compute utilisation. The limit: at very long contexts cache reads dominate, and splitting the world into two phases stops explaining what you observe.

Read: [Optimizing inference](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/llm_optims)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="inf-continuous-batching"></a>7. Explain iteration-level batching and how requests enter and leave a running inference batch.

*Knowledge · [Inference, serving and cost](../themes/inference-economics.md) · [Checklist](../themes/inference-economics.md#inf-continuous-batching)*

The scheduler rebuilds the batch at every generation step instead of waiting for everyone to finish: a new sequence joins at the next iteration boundary, and one that emitted a stop token or hit its length limit leaves immediately and frees the slot. That way utilisation doesn't collapse because of one long answer. We pay with scheduler complexity and the risk that some requests get preempted or wait longer than the rest. What you cap is not the number of requests but the total tokens per step and the available KV memory, otherwise the cache pool runs dry and you start evicting and recomputing. I'd watch not only throughput but time to first token, the distribution of queue wait and the share of requests that waited past a threshold. A scheduler doesn't cure overload: with sustained excess demand you need rejection or degradation, not a cleverer queue.

Read: [Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.06180)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="inf-speculation"></a>8. Explain exact speculative decoding, its acceptance step and workloads where the draft model adds overhead instead of speed.

*Knowledge · [Inference, serving and cost](../themes/inference-economics.md) · [Checklist](../themes/inference-economics.md#inf-speculation)*

The scheme is this: a cheap draft model generates several tokens ahead, and the target model verifies them in one parallel pass, confirming several positions within its single step. Accuracy is preserved honestly: each proposed token is accepted by comparing the target and draft probabilities, and on rejection the token is resampled from a corrected distribution, so the final distribution matches the target model's. The gain is set by three quantities: the average share of accepted tokens, the cost of running the draft, and spare compute available for verification. I'd measure the average number of accepted tokens per pass and end to end latency with and without the draft model on my own workload, not on a demo example. Large compute-bound batches leave less spare compute; draft-target mismatch lowers acceptance. Either can erase the speedup or cause a slowdown.

Read: [Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.17192)

### <a id="inf-memory-budget"></a>9. Estimate a serving memory budget for a 70-billion-parameter model, explicitly choosing precision, context and concurrency assumptions.

*Applied scenario · [Inference, serving and cost](../themes/inference-economics.md) · [Checklist](../themes/inference-economics.md#inf-memory-budget)*

I would state a hypothetical architecture before budgeting: 70 billion parameters, 80 layers, eight KV heads and head width 128. BF16 weights occupy about 140 GB; int8 roughly 70 GB and four-bit roughly 35 GB, excluding quantisation metadata. For BF16 KV, bytes equal 2 times concurrency times layers times tokens times KV heads times head width times two. Choosing 8,192 tokens and four concurrent sequences gives 10 GiB of KV cache. On two hypothetical 80 GiB accelerators, tensor parallelism could split weights and KV heads, leaving roughly 9.8 GiB per device for activations, buffers, fragmentation and headroom. I would verify actual usable memory and peak allocations, then lower concurrency if needed. This is a capacity estimate, not evidence that the configuration meets a latency SLO.

Read: [Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.06180)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="inf-cost-reduction"></a>10. You are asked to reduce serving cost by an order of magnitude. Rank the levers and explain how you would test whether that target is achievable.

*Applied scenario · [Inference, serving and cost](../themes/inference-economics.md) · [Checklist](../themes/inference-economics.md#inf-cost-reduction)*

First I fix the metric: not price per million tokens, but the cost of one successfully completed task at a given quality and SLO, otherwise any saving turns into a quiet product regression. Then the levers in decreasing order of expected effect: a smaller model or a distilled one where quality holds; cutting context and reusing work, meaning prompt caching and caching of repeated answers; server side measures such as continuous batching and decent utilisation; and only then quantisation and precision work. The first levers reduce work and the last reduce price per unit, and their ceilings differ. I'd turn each change on separately, measuring quality on an eval set and latency at the tails. An important limit: a tenfold saving rarely comes from one lever, and if the product of honestly measured effects falls short, say so before the work starts.

Read: [Optimizing inference](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/llm_optims) · [Site Reliability Engineering](https://sre.google/sre-book/table-of-contents/)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="inf-tail-regression"></a>11. After a deployment, p99 latency doubles although model weights are unchanged. How do you isolate the cause?

*Applied scenario · [Inference, serving and cost](../themes/inference-economics.md) · [Checklist](../themes/inference-economics.md#inf-tail-regression)*

With unchanged weights, I examine traffic, scheduling and infrastructure. First I compare prompt and output lengths, request types and new clients before and after release. On slow request traces, I inspect queueing, prefill, decode and dependency durations; adding separate stage p99 values would not give end-to-end p99. Then I check prompt-cache hits, batch sizes, KV evictions, dependency tails and saturation of memory, bandwidth and threads, including neighbouring workloads. I change one factor at a time to keep effects distinguishable. A rollback provides useful evidence, but causal confidence requires comparable traffic and conditions, ideally a controlled canary. I would verify that both the workload mix and tail latency recover before attributing the regression to a release. Several bottlenecks can contribute, so there may be no single cause.

Read: [The Tail at Scale](https://research.google/pubs/the-tail-at-scale/)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="rag-chunking"></a>12. Choose a chunking approach for technical documentation, including how you preserve meaning across section boundaries.

*Applied scenario · [RAG and retrieval](../themes/rag-retrieval.md) · [Checklist](../themes/rag-retrieval.md#rag-chunking)*

For documentation I'd split along the document structure rather than by a fixed character count: the unit's a section or subsection, and into the chunk I carry the chain of headings, the document identifier and the position inside it. Then the fragment stays intelligible away from its page, and I can return an exact link to it. The trade-off is direct: small chunks match the query more precisely but lose context, large ones keep the meaning but blur the embedding and drag surplus text into the prompt. I don't guess size and overlap, I tune them on a set of representative questions, comparing retrieval misses against final answer quality. Separately I'd check tables, code examples, and cases where the answer sits on the boundary between two chunks. Splitting won't save you if the documentation is contradictory or stale, and it doesn't replace adding explanatory context to a fragment before indexing.

Read: [Contextual Retrieval in AI Systems](https://www.anthropic.com/news/contextual-retrieval)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="rag-hybrid"></a>13. When would you combine lexical and dense retrieval, and how would you merge their rankings?

*Knowledge · [RAG and retrieval](../themes/rag-retrieval.md) · [Checklist](../themes/rag-retrieval.md#rag-hybrid)*

It's worth combining when queries contain both exact strings and free wording. Lexical search is irreplaceable for identifiers, error codes, function names, versions and rare terms that an embedding doesn't distinguish; dense search pulls in paraphrases and synonyms where there's no word overlap at all. You can't add their scores together directly: a lexical score isn't normalised and isn't comparable with cosine similarity. It's more practical to fuse by rank, for instance reciprocal rank fusion, or to normalise within a single query, or to take the union of candidates and rerank with a cross-encoder, at which point the original scales stop mattering entirely. I'd test on a fixed query set with labelled relevance, switching off each branch and the reranking in turn to see what each part contributes. The price is a second index, an extra latency stage and cost. If queries are homogeneous, hybrid adds complexity without a gain.

Read: [Contextual Retrieval in AI Systems](https://www.anthropic.com/news/contextual-retrieval)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="rag-stage-evaluation"></a>14. How would you separately evaluate document retrieval and answer generation in a RAG application?

*Applied scenario · [RAG and retrieval](../themes/rag-retrieval.md) · [Checklist](../themes/rag-retrieval.md#rag-stage-evaluation)*

For representative questions I label answer-bearing passages and define acceptable answers separately. Retrieval is then measured by its own metrics, whether the needed passage appeared in the results and at what rank, and generation by groundedness, whether every statement rests on the context it was given, and by factual correctness. The key move is running generation with the gold passages as input: if the answer is right with them, retrieval or context assembly needs investigation; if not, the problem is the model, the prompt or the context format. Without that split, an end to end metric mixes two different defects and the team fixes the wrong stage. I'd keep the set small but alive, topping it up with real production failures. Limits: relevance labelling is subjective, gold passages don't reproduce the noise of real retrieval, and a judge model itself needs checking against human agreement.

Read: [Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401) · [Demystifying evals for AI agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents)

### <a id="rag-permissions"></a>15. Design retrieval that enforces the source system's access rights, including permission changes and shared caches.

*System design · [RAG and retrieval](../themes/rag-retrieval.md) · [Checklist](../themes/rag-retrieval.md#rag-permissions)*

The source system defines document permissions; retrieval must enforce them before content reaches the model. I pass the user's identity into search and filter candidates by access, then check authoritative permissions if indexed ACL freshness cannot be established. Post-filtering can damage recall, and applying controls only after generation is too late. Permission changes and deletions need measurable propagation, revoked grants must invalidate caches, and cached answers must respect the current caller's access. A shared embedding cache need not be per user if it cannot expose restricted content and retrieval remains authorised. I test revoked access, deleted documents and users without rights, including citations, suggestions and logs. Stale content can be labelled; uncertain authorisation must fail closed rather than merely display a warning.

Read: [Document-level access control](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/search/search-document-level-access-overview)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="rag-ann-index"></a>16. Compare exact search, HNSW and IVF-PQ for an embedding index under memory, recall and latency constraints.

*Knowledge · [RAG and retrieval](../themes/rag-retrieval.md) · [Checklist](../themes/rag-retrieval.md#rag-ann-index)*

I'd start with exact search over a sample of queries: it gives the baseline against which the word recall means anything at all. HNSW builds a multi layer graph of neighbours and descends it greedily: search is fast and accurate, insertion is cheap, but the graph lives entirely in memory and costs dearly there. IVF-PQ first divides the space into coarse clusters and looks at only the nearest few, storing vectors compressed by product quantisers: it needs several times less memory, but quantisation itself loses accuracy and the clustering has to be trained on representative data. I'd choose by measuring recall against the exact baseline at the target latency, and separately measure memory footprint, the cost of updates and deletions, and behaviour under metadata filters. A small collection needs no approximate index at all, and no index will fix bad embeddings.

Read: [Efficient and robust approximate nearest neighbor search using Hierarchical Navigable Small World graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.09320) · [Faiss indexes](https://github.com/facebookresearch/faiss/wiki/Faiss-indexes)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="agt-react"></a>17. What does interleaving reasoning with tool observations add to a language-model agent compared with reasoning alone?

*Knowledge · [Agents, tools and protocols](../themes/agents-tools.md) · [Checklist](../themes/agents-tools.md#agt-react)*

Interleaving gives the model what its own reasoning cannot: a planned action and an observation returned by the environment are different things, and the observation can interrupt a chain of plausible but wrong assumptions. The mechanism is simple. The model states a step, calls a tool, gets a result, and builds the next step on it, so an observation can disconfirm a bad hypothesis before the final answer. You pay in latency and cost: every round is another call and more context, and tools return errors, empty results and junk the model must tell apart from fact. I would measure the share of tasks where an observation changed the plan, and the share of steps spent repeating one call. The limit: external feedback helps only while the environment answers honestly. If a tool is silently wrong, the loop only entrenches the error more confidently.

Read: [ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03629)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="agt-retries"></a>18. Design recovery from tool errors and timeouts, including cases where a timed-out call may already have changed external state.

*System design · [Agents, tools and protocols](../themes/agents-tools.md) · [Checklist](../themes/agents-tools.md#agt-retries)*

Before retrying, I classify the outcome: transient failure, permanent failure or ambiguous completion. A timeout on a write is ambiguous because the operation may still be running or already committed. For writes, I persist a client-generated idempotency key with the task and reuse it under the provider's documented guarantees. Without that guarantee, a state read alone is insufficient: it may be stale while the original operation remains in flight. I require an authoritative terminal outcome or reconciliation; otherwise I stop automated retries. Safe retries have an attempt budget, overall deadline and exponential backoff with jitter. When that budget expires, I escalate with the operation history and unresolved status. Idempotency depends on provider semantics, retention and key scope; merely attaching a key does not make a write safe.

Read: [Designing robust and predictable APIs with idempotency](https://stripe.com/blog/idempotency)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="agt-tool-surface"></a>19. How would you select, name and document tools so that a model chooses the right operation and arguments?

*System design · [Agents, tools and protocols](../themes/agents-tools.md) · [Checklist](../themes/agents-tools.md#agt-tool-surface)*

I design a tool as one coherent operation the model picks by a single clear name, not as a thin wrapper over an endpoint. The name states intent, the schema stays minimal and checkable, with enumerations instead of free text wherever the options are finite, so a bad argument is rejected by validation, not by the downstream system. Results need bounds: return the relevant fields and a sensible volume, otherwise the context fills with noise and the next choice gets worse. Write errors so the next step follows from them, not just a code. I test this on realistic tasks: run a set of requests, measure how often the right tool and the right arguments were chosen, then remove near-identical operations the model confuses. A description can't replace a missing operation, and if the action is not in the set, the model will improvise it out of unsuitable ones.

Read: [Writing effective tools for AI agents—using AI agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="agt-termination"></a>20. Define completion and stopping conditions for an agent loop so it cannot spend indefinitely on an unfinished task.

*System design · [Agents, tools and protocols](../themes/agents-tools.md) · [Checklist](../themes/agents-tools.md#agt-termination)*

The loop has to end in an explicit terminal state, and there are several: success, blocked, cancelled by the user, and budget exhausted. They cannot be merged, because the response differs: success closes the task, blocked needs a human, and budget exhausted says honestly that we never learned whether the task was doable. I define progress from observable state in the environment, not from the model's confidence, and alongside it I keep hard limits on steps, money and time; without them an agent will cycle through options forever on an unsolvable task. The cost is obvious: some genuinely long tasks get cut off, so on stopping you save state, what was done and which side effects are already applied, so a resume or handoff does not repeat them. The limit: budgets bound spend, not quality, and an agent can stop on time with a formally complete but useless result.

Read: [Building Effective AI Agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="agt-approval"></a>21. Design human approval for consequential agent actions, including how approval remains bound to the exact action being executed.

*System design · [Agents, tools and protocols](../themes/agents-tools.md) · [Checklist](../themes/agents-tools.md#agt-approval)*

Approval works only if the person sees the concrete action, not the intent: recipient, amount, object and how reversible the consequences are, exactly as they will go to the external system. So permission binds not to the conversation or the session but to the validated arguments of one specific call: we freeze them, show them, and at execution recheck the initiator's rights and that fields are unchanged. If the model changed even one material argument after approval, the old permission is void and a new one is requested. I make execution idempotent so a retry after a network failure is not a second charge, and I log the decision, its author, time and result. The limit: this protects against mistaken and externally prompted actions, but under a stream of requests it degenerates into a formality: people approve without looking, so only actions whose cost of error is real deserve it.

Read: [Building Effective AI Agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents) · [Designing robust and predictable APIs with idempotency](https://stripe.com/blog/idempotency)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="pt-rlhf"></a>22. Walk through a preference-based RLHF pipeline and explain the roles of the reward model and reference-policy penalty.

*Knowledge · [Fine-tuning and post-training](../themes/post-training.md) · [Checklist](../themes/post-training.md#pt-rlhf)*

RLHF splits into three stages that differ by data. First demonstrations: examples of desired answers, on which the base model is finetuned with supervised learning. Then preference pairs: a person sees several answers to one prompt and ranks them, and on those comparisons you train a reward model, a separate model predicting which answer a person picks. In the third stage the policy is optimised against that reward on its own rollouts, with a penalty for diverging from the reference model added to the objective, usually a KL divergence; without it the policy drifts to where reward is high and the text has degraded. That is the trade-off: push harder on reward and you reach its overoptimisation sooner. Check on held-out human preferences, not on the reward itself, and watch how divergence from the reference tracks the real gain. The reward model inherits annotator bias, and optimisation amplifies it.

Read: [Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.02155)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="pt-dpo"></a>23. Compare DPO with PPO-based RLHF, including the assumptions behind offline preference learning and reasons to collect fresh rollouts.

*Knowledge · [Fine-tuning and post-training](../themes/post-training.md) · [Checklist](../themes/post-training.md#pt-dpo)*

DPO derives a preference loss using log policy-to-reference probability ratios, equivalently differences of log probabilities. It compares those quantities for preferred and rejected responses, avoiding a separately trained reward model and an online rollout loop. That simplifies implementation, though the frozen reference still contributes to the objective. Standard offline DPO learns from a fixed preference dataset. If its coverage misses responses the updated policy produces, the training signal may generalise poorly there. PPO can score current rollouts with a reward model, but that model can also fail outside its training distribution. I would therefore inspect preference coverage, held-out behaviour and policy drift before choosing between them. A simpler loss does not make online RL obsolete: the decision depends on data coverage, compute budget and the amount of behavioural change required.

Read: [Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18290)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="pt-lora"></a>24. Derive the low-rank weight update used by LoRA and propose an experiment for choosing its rank.

*Knowledge · [Fine-tuning and post-training](../themes/post-training.md) · [Checklist](../themes/post-training.md#pt-lora)*

LoRA freezes the original weight matrix and trains a low-rank correction instead: ΔW = BA, where B is d by r, A is r by k, and r is much smaller than both d and k. Instead of d times k trainable parameters you are left with r times the sum of d and k, orders of magnitude fewer at small rank, and at inference the correction can be merged into the base weights with no extra latency. The constraint is that rank sets capacity: too small an r simply can't hold the behaviour change you need. The experiment is straightforward. Fix the data and the set of target modules, vary only r over a grid, and compare quality on held-out tasks while checking for regressions in general capability. Merging the adapter is convenient, but it gives up keeping several adapters on one base and switching them per request.

Read: [LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.09685)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="pt-qlora"></a>25. How does QLoRA reduce finetuning memory, and which tensors remain trainable or require higher precision?

*Knowledge · [Fine-tuning and post-training](../themes/post-training.md) · [Checklist](../themes/post-training.md#pt-qlora)*

QLoRA saves memory by keeping base weights quantised to four bits and frozen while only low-rank adapters are trained: gradients and optimiser states exist for those alone, and they were exactly what ate most of the memory in full finetuning. Three mechanisms work together: NF4, a quantisation format designed for normally distributed weights; double quantisation, which compresses the quantisation constants themselves; and paged optimisers, which move optimiser states into host memory during spikes. You pay in compute, because weights are dequantised to the compute precision on every matrix multiply, which can slow training depending on implementation. Activation memory does not go anywhere and grows with sequence length and batch size, so on long context it becomes the binding constraint again. The limit: this is a way to fit finetuning into less memory, not a way to guarantee full-finetuning quality on any task.

Read: [QLoRA: Efficient Finetuning of Quantized LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14314)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="pt-method-choice"></a>26. Choose between prompt changes, retrieval and finetuning for a failing AI feature; include data freshness, latency and total cost.

*Applied scenario · [Fine-tuning and post-training](../themes/post-training.md) · [Checklist](../themes/post-training.md#pt-method-choice)*

I find the cause of the failures first, because three different diseases are cured differently: the model lacks knowledge, the task was explained badly, or it has persistent unwanted behaviour and format. Going through a sample of real failures is cheaper than any training. Bad instructions are fixed by the prompt, which is always the baseline everything else is compared against. Missing fresh or private knowledge is covered by retrieval: data updates without retraining, answers get source citations, and you pay in search latency and index quality. I take finetuning once enough representative examples of the wanted behaviour have accumulated, and count the full cost: labelling, training, version maintenance, and repeating all of it when the base model changes. I decide on a held-out set, not on impressions. The limit: finetuning barely helps with facts going stale, and retrieval will not fix behaviour if the model ignores what it found.

Read: [Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401) · [LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.09685)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="eval-judge"></a>27. Design an LLM judge and a calibration process that exposes order, verbosity and self-preference biases.

*System design · [Evaluation and observability](../themes/evals-observability.md) · [Checklist](../themes/evals-observability.md#eval-judge)*

A judge starts not with a prompt but with criteria: what counts as a good answer in this task, written so that two people would agree. Then you need a held-out calibration set with human labels; it measures the judge itself, otherwise we are simply trusting a model to grade a model. The known biases are checked by experiment: run each pair in both orders and see whether the verdict flips; compare the length of the winning answers to catch a reward for verbosity; hide authorship and check whether answers from the judge's own family win systematically. I would track agreement between judge and people, the share of pairs where swapping order changes the decision, and send unreliable cases to experts. The limit: a judge measures conformance to criteria, not usefulness to the user, and wherever an answer can be checked deterministically an ordinary check is cheaper.

Read: [Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.05685)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="eval-release-gate"></a>28. Design a release gate for prompt and model updates, including what happens when aggregate gains hide a critical regression.

*System design · [Evaluation and observability](../themes/evals-observability.md) · [Checklist](../themes/evals-observability.md#eval-release-gate)*

Admitting a change means comparing the candidate against a pinned baseline, so first version everything: the prompt, the model and its parameters, the dataset, and the grader code. Without that you can't tell what to attribute the gain to. I set the acceptance rule as a set of conditions rather than one average: the aggregate is no worse than baseline and no critical slice has dropped, meaning safety, money, and rare but expensive scenarios. Otherwise an overall rise quietly hides a regression on a small but important group. I handle stochasticity with repeated runs and look at the spread, not one pass. Offline scores are not enough: next comes a controlled rollout on a share of traffic with rollback conditions written down in advance, so nobody argues about them mid-incident. A gate catches only what the dataset covers, so new failure modes appear after they have already happened in production.

Read: [Demystifying evals for AI agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="eval-benchmark-mismatch"></a>29. Benchmark results improve but users report a worse product. What hypotheses would you test first?

*Applied scenario · [Evaluation and observability](../themes/evals-observability.md) · [Checklist](../themes/evals-observability.md#eval-benchmark-mismatch)*

The first hypothesis is a gap between what the benchmark measures and what people actually do in the product. I would take a sample of live traffic and line it up against the test set by task type, language and length; often the category that improved barely occurs in the product. The second hypothesis is test leakage into training, or fitting to the set. The third is a regression on a specific slice hidden by the average. The fourth is non-benchmark causes: latency went up, the answer format changed, expectations shifted after the update. There is one practical step: reproduce specific complaints as test cases and add typical failures to the set, and the conversation moves from impressions to measurement. The limit: grow the set carefully, because optimising straight at it will detach the metric from usefulness again, and some complaints are not about the model at all.

Read: [Rules of Machine Learning](https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/guides/rules-of-ml)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="eval-traces"></a>30. Design observability for a production LLM workflow: which spans, versions, costs and feedback should be linked?

*System design · [Evaluation and observability](../themes/evals-observability.md) · [Checklist](../themes/evals-observability.md#eval-traces)*

The core of observability is one end-to-end task identifier that every span attaches to: model calls, retrieval steps, tool calls, with the prompt, model, index and code versions alongside. Without versions a trace shows what broke but will not answer which change broke it. On each span I record latency, tokens and cost, the outcome and the error code, and I collect user feedback on a sample and bind it to the same identifier. Request and response contents are sensitive data, so I keep them selectively, with a short retention and masked fields, while metrics and structure can live longer. From there the traces show at which stage the task is lost, and recurring failures move into the eval set as cases. The limit: a trace explains one failure but says nothing about how frequent it is until there are aggregates beside it.

Read: [Site Reliability Engineering](https://sre.google/sre-book/table-of-contents/) · [Demystifying evals for AI agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="eval-agent-outcomes"></a>31. How should evaluation of a tool-using agent differ from grading one generated response?

*System design · [Evaluation and observability](../themes/evals-observability.md) · [Checklist](../themes/evals-observability.md#eval-agent-outcomes)*

The main difference: an agent has a result in the environment, and that is what you check, not the text in which it reported success. Saying it is done costs nothing, so evaluation reads the final state: was the record created, was the mail sent, what status is the ticket in. The second dimension is the trajectory: a task can be completed at the cost of extra calls, wasted money, or a dangerous action like deletion, and that is graded separately from completion, otherwise a bad path is masked by a good outcome. The third is repeatability: one lucky run proves nothing; you need several trials from the same clean environment state and a measured success rate, because the agent is non-deterministic. The limit: all this needs isolated environments with reproducible state; they are expensive and always poorer than reality, so some failure modes appear only in production.

Read: [Demystifying evals for AI agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="mm-visual-input"></a>32. Compare projection layers, cross-attention and token-based integration for giving a language model access to images.

*Knowledge · [Multimodal and voice](../themes/multimodal-voice.md) · [Checklist](../themes/multimodal-voice.md#mm-visual-input)*

Two choices matter: the image encoder and its interface to the language model. The encoder is usually taken off the shelf; the fork is at the interface. A projection maps patches into tokens of the language model's space and they simply take their place in the shared sequence: simple to build, fits many decoder architectures, but every visual token occupies context window and compute time. Cross-attention leaves visual features outside and adds cross-attention layers into the blocks, as in Flamingo: the text sequence doesn't grow, but you have to change the architecture and train new layers. The choice is decided by the visual token budget: fine detail, text inside the image and high resolution demand either more tokens or tiling. I'd compare the options on tasks needing spatial precision, not on general descriptions. Either way an alignment stage is required: without training on pairs the modalities won't meet.

Read: [Flamingo: a Visual Language Model for Few-Shot Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.14198)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="mm-accents"></a>33. How would you improve and evaluate speech recognition for mixed-language utterances and different accents?

*Applied scenario · [Multimodal and voice](../themes/multimodal-voice.md) · [Checklist](../themes/multimodal-voice.md#mm-accents)*

You start not with the model but with sliced evaluation: an overall WER on an averaged set hides exactly the groups the work exists for. I'd build separate slices by language, by accent and region, by level and type of noise, and by utterances that switch language mid phrase, making sure each slice holds enough different speakers. Then task level metrics, not just WER: are names, amounts, numbers and the other entities that an action depends on recognised correctly, since one corrupted digit costs more than a dozen small errors. Improvement usually comes from data and adaptation: fine-tuning on the domain, a glossary of terms in the prompt, text normalisation. I check the result on held out speakers and domains, otherwise we get memorisation rather than robustness. A model that is strong on average can easily sag on one particular accent, and the labelling itself can be biased too.

Read: [Robust Speech Recognition via Large-Scale Weak Supervision](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.04356)

### <a id="sd-enterprise-rag"></a>34. Design a knowledge assistant over ten million enterprise documents with per-user permissions and a continuously changing corpus.

*System design · [AI system design](../themes/ai-system-design.md) · [Checklist](../themes/ai-system-design.md#sd-enterprise-rag)*

I clarify peak query volume, content freshness requirements and permission semantics before sizing. The ingestion path versions documents, chunks them, computes embeddings and attaches access metadata. The online path obtains the user's current identity and groups, filters retrieval and supplies authorised context to generation with source citations. Indexing delay and access revocation are separate concerns: stale content may be disclosed, but stale ACLs cannot justify leaking a revoked document. I require bounded authorisation freshness or an authoritative permission check before context leaves retrieval; when neither is available, access fails closed. Cached grants and answers must be invalidated or revalidated. I test grounding and revocation separately, including concurrent permission changes and cache hits. Search outages and reduced coverage should be visible to users without weakening the access boundary.

Read: [Document-level access control](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/search/search-document-level-access-overview) · [Contextual Retrieval in AI Systems](https://www.anthropic.com/news/contextual-retrieval)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="sd-gateway"></a>35. Design an LLM gateway with provider routing, failover, caching, rate limits and enforceable spending budgets.

*System design · [AI system design](../themes/ai-system-design.md) · [Checklist](../themes/ai-system-design.md#sd-gateway)*

A gateway exists for one contract over different providers, so first I describe their capabilities, streaming output, tool calling, context limits, behaviour on failure, and unify only genuinely compatible semantics; the rest I expose explicitly rather than emulate, otherwise the client quietly gets different behaviour. Quotas and budgets I check before dispatch, per client, and they must account for retries, or failover eats the budget itself; when a budget is exhausted I return a clear error saying when to try again. The cache key includes the model and its parameters, otherwise the cache serves an answer from another model. The subtlest part is the failover boundary: once part of a response has gone to the client you cannot switch providers without breaking the stream, and a side-effecting call cannot be repeated without idempotency. The limit: a gateway levels interfaces and failures, but not the quality gap between models.

Read: [Scaling your API with rate limiters](https://stripe.com/blog/rate-limiters) · [Designing robust and predictable APIs with idempotency](https://stripe.com/blog/idempotency)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="sd-support-agent"></a>36. Design a customer-support agent that can execute service actions and transfer the case to a human when needed.

*System design · [AI system design](../themes/ai-system-design.md) · [Checklist](../themes/ai-system-design.md#sd-support-agent)*

I start from which requests the agent serves and turn them into an explicit tool list with permission boundaries: it checks order status itself, issues a refund up to an amount threshold and with confirmation, and anything else is outside its authority. A narrow surface buys predictability at the cost of requests it will not close. Against duplicate actions you have case state and observed operation outcomes: before issuing a refund the agent checks whether one was already issued, and writing calls carry an idempotency key. I define escalation conditions in advance from observable signals: the customer asks for a human, the task is outside the tool set, a tool returned an ambiguous outcome, the conversation got heated. On transfer the person gets the history, actions taken and their results, so they don't start from scratch. The agent removes routine load, but on complex, emotional cases its value is small.

Read: [Building Effective AI Agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents) · [Writing effective tools for AI agents—using AI agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="sd-consumer-chat"></a>37. Design a streaming chat service for hundreds of millions of users, including capacity, conversation storage and graceful overload behaviour.

*System design · [AI system design](../themes/ai-system-design.md) · [Checklist](../themes/ai-system-design.md#sd-consumer-chat)*

I start the estimate from explicit assumptions about traffic: how many users are active at peak, how many concurrent streams they hold, the average answer length in tokens and the generation speed required. From those you derive the needed throughput in tokens per second and the number of concurrent sessions, and from conversation length and lifetime, the storage volume. The actual numbers depend on the product, so what is valuable is not the number itself but that it was derived from an assumption somebody can challenge. Architecturally I separate three layers: admission control with a queue and priorities, inference scheduling with batching and preemption, and conversation storage in an ordinary database, apart from compute. Cancellation is mandatory: the user left, generation stops and frees memory. Under overload I reject fast and explicitly. The limit: headroom costs money, and under a sustained accelerator shortage degraded service is unavoidable.

Read: [Site Reliability Engineering](https://sre.google/sre-book/table-of-contents/) · [Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.06180)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="code-causal-attention"></a>38. Implement scaled dot-product attention with a causal mask and tests that would expose attention to future tokens.

*Coding · [Practical coding](../themes/coding-practical.md) · [Checklist](../themes/coding-practical.md#code-causal-attention)*

I'd start with an explicit contract on dimensions: batch, heads, length, head width, with a shape check at the entry, because most bugs here are swapped axes and silent broadcasting. Then scores as Q times K transposed on the last axis, division by the square root of head width, minus infinity at future positions j &gt; i, allowing the diagonal and past, a stable softmax that subtracts the row maximum, and multiplication by V. The mask has to come before softmax: zeroing the weights after normalisation is wrong, the sum is spoiled by future positions. I'd write two kinds of test: a tiny example with numbers worked out by hand, and a causality test that changes tokens after a position and confirms the outputs before it didn't move. Separately I'd check a fully masked row. This is a teaching implementation: no memory saving like flash attention, and no inference caching.

Read: [Attention Is All You Need](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="code-token-bucket"></a>39. Implement a token-bucket limiter and explain what must change when several workers enforce the same limit.

*Coding · [Practical coding](../themes/coding-practical.md) · [Checklist](../themes/coding-practical.md#code-token-bucket)*

The bucket stores a token count and last refill time. On each call I measure elapsed time on a monotonic clock, add elapsed time times the refill rate, clip at capacity, and deduct what was asked for if there's enough. Capacity sets the burst you allow and the rate sets the average pace, the main trade-off. Avoid wall-clock time: a clock change or a sync will give a negative interval or hand out a full bucket. Check and deduct must be one atomic operation under a lock, otherwise two threads see the same last token. I'd test a burst on a full bucket, refusal on an empty one, and recovery after the right interval, injecting a fake clock instead of waiting. A shared limit across workers needs an external counter with a script that refills and deducts atomically, or the quota split per worker: cheaper, less exact at the boundaries.

Read: [Scaling your API with rate limiters](https://stripe.com/blog/rate-limiters)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="code-async-batches"></a>40. Write an asynchronous API batch processor with bounded concurrency, retry jitter and isolated per-item failures.

*Coding · [Practical coding](../themes/coding-practical.md) · [Checklist](../themes/coding-practical.md#code-async-batches)*

I use an input queue, a semaphore on the number of concurrent requests, a wrapper around each item that catches its own exceptions and returns either a result or an error, and collection of all outcomes in input order. Cancellation and an overall deadline are passed inward, so that when time runs out the in-flight requests are cancelled too, not only those waiting in the queue. Retry only what is sensible to retry: timeouts, network failures, rate limit responses and server errors, with bounded attempts, exponential backoff and jitter, since without spread the clients synchronise and hit in a wave. For unsafe methods a retry needs an idempotency key, otherwise you get duplicates. One item's failure must not sink the batch, so I return a status per input. I'd test partial success, a permanent error, the deadline firing, and cancellation halfway. Client retries amplify overload, so the cap is mandatory.

Read: [Designing robust and predictable APIs with idempotency](https://stripe.com/blog/idempotency) · [Site Reliability Engineering](https://sre.google/sre-book/table-of-contents/)
